title: Two languages in one country: patterns and forces

readings.title: Languages spoken at home by province of Country A

parts.label: A
parts.demand: Give the information asked for: a word or short phrase can earn the point, with no reasons needed.
parts.prompt: Identify the scale of analysis of the data shown on the map.

rubric.point: Identifies the scale as subnational (local or regional within the country): one value for each province.

parts.sample: The data are at the subnational scale: the map gives one value for each province of Country A.

parts.label: B
parts.demand: Give the relevant characteristics: what it is like, where and how much. A name alone earns nothing.
parts.prompt: Describe the pattern of Language B shown on the map.

rubric.point: Describes where and how much: Language B is concentrated in the east and southeast (90% or more in the Eastern Plains and South Coast) and falls to under 10% in the west.
accept: highest in the Eastern Plains and South Coast

parts.sample: Language B is concentrated in the east: 90% or more of people speak it at home in the Eastern Plains and South Coast, half or more do in the Lake District, and under 10% do in the Western Uplands and Northern Hills.

parts.label: C
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how Language B can act as a centripetal force within the eastern provinces.

rubric.point: Explains that a shared language links people in the east (schools, media, daily life), so it unites them.
accept: shared language builds a shared identity and communication in the east

parts.sample: In the Eastern Plains almost everyone speaks Language B at home, so people share schools, radio, songs and daily conversation in one language, which builds a common identity that pulls them together.

parts.label: D
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how the language difference shown on the map can act as a centrifugal force for Country A as a whole.

rubric.point: Explains that two languages concentrated in separate regions weaken national unity, with the link stated.
accept: eastern speakers feel apart from a mostly Language A government
separate media and parties by language region

parts.sample: At the national scale, Language B speakers live mostly in the east while Language A dominates the rest, so each region has its own language, media and leaders, which leads people in the east to feel less connected to the national government and pulls the country apart.

parts.label: E
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how speakers of Language B could use placemaking to build a sense of place in the Eastern Plains.

rubric.point: Explains a placemaking act (signs, murals, festivals, monuments in Language B) and how it builds identity or belonging.
accept: street signs or murals in Language B
a yearly festival of Language B music

parts.sample: Speakers could put up street signs and murals in Language B and hold a yearly festival of songs in their language, so the landscape itself tells residents and visitors that the Eastern Plains is a Language B place, which strengthens their sense of belonging.

parts.label: F
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how making both Language A and Language B official languages could act as a centripetal force for Country A.

rubric.point: Explains that official status lets Language B speakers use their language with the government, so they feel included and the pull apart weakens.
accept: equal use in courts, schools and government
speakers of B feel respected and included

parts.sample: If both languages were official, Language B speakers in the east could use their own language in courts, schools and government offices, so they would feel included as full members of Country A, which would weaken the pull to separate.

parts.label: G
parts.demand: State the degree first (to a high, moderate or low degree), then explain why with evidence.
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which the language pattern on the map could lead to devolution in Country A.

rubric.point: States a degree, then explains it: the concentration of Language B in the east gives a region with its own identity that may seek more self-rule, weighed against what could reduce that pressure.
accept: to a moderate or high degree, with the regional concentration as reason
to a limited degree, if bilingual policy or shared ties reduce the pull

parts.sample: To a moderate degree: because Language B speakers are concentrated in the east, they form a region with its own identity that could demand more power from the capital, but the mixed Capital Region and a bilingual policy could keep ties to the rest of Country A strong, so full devolution is not certain.
